Figure 60. Hour VMT fractions by FleetDNA vocation for combination-unit short-haul vehicles Figure 61 displays the vocational VMT fractions for single-unit short-haul vehicles from FleetDNA. Single-unit food delivery vehicles drive proportionally more in the early morning hours around hour ID 5 (4 a.m.) than their combination-unit counterparts. Towing vehicles drive mostly between 10 a.m. and 8 p.m. on weekday urban roads. On weekends, towing trucks drive heavily between midnight and 4 a.m. Snowplows operate at all hours of the day and join food delivery and weekend towing for the very early morning cycles. However, most other vocations such as parcel, linen, and warehouse delivery begin around 6 a.m. All three vocations peak around 9 a.m. on weekday urban driving. Hour VMT fractions by FleetDNA vocation for single-unit short-haul vehicles 5.2.3.2 CE-CERT VMT Distribution by Hour ID We now look at the CE-CERT data set VMT distributions by hour ID. Except for other buses (airport shuttles), of which there were only four and may not constitute enough data to change MOVES3 national averages, the other four source types in CE-CERT are in common with FleetDNA, and we will hold recommendations until the following section on combined data. Here we will just make some notes of comparison to MOVES3. Figure 62 shows how combination-unit short-haul CE-CERT vehicles compare to MOVES3. Similar to Figure 55, on rural freeways on weekdays, CE-CERT has little peaks at hour IDs 4 and 6, but they are less pronounced than FleetDNA’s. Then the distributions differ more; whereas FleetDNA spikes at hour ID 8, CE-CERT enters a lull. CE-CERT displays a much cleaner high peak around noon, temporally in advance of MOVES3’s second bimodal peak, and in contrast to FleetDNA’s low miles driven during this time. FleetDNA has an additional late evening spike and in general looks choppier. The smoother signal of CE-CERT on rural freeways may be due to FleetDNA having less recorded driving time at a maximum of 6 hours per hour ID to CE-CERT’s 30 hours. Both data sets also have a cautionary data classification for urban freeways on weekends. Although the shape of the distributions differ, in both data sets the trucks travel most miles in the morning hours and less in the evening, which contrasts the default MOVES3 distribution. For urban freeways on weekdays, both FleetDNA and CE-CERT peak before the first MOVES3 peak and do not display the bimodal distribution that is characteristic of MOVES3 weekday defaults.
